 Real history, figures inspire tvN drama '100 Days of Deception'
 Listen Listen Text Size Print Summary
 Close summary Set in 1932 during Japanese colonial rule, tvN’s 100 Days of Deception follows pickpocket Lee Ga-kyung as she is forced to join the independence group Gugukdan and infiltrate the Japanese Government-General of Korea. The drama draws on the 1919 Jeam-ri Massacre and the work of journalists Frank W. Schofield and Albert Taylor. Its fictional mansion Huiwon pays tribute to Taylor’s Seoul home, Dilkusha.
 Key Facts
 The Jeam-ri Massacre took place on April 15, 1919, in what is now Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province.
 Historical records say 29 people were killed, including 23 at Jeam Church and six in nearby Goju-ri.
 Frank W. Schofield’s report The Massacre of Chai-Amm-Ni appeared in The Shanghai Gazette on May 27, 1919.
 Schofield received the Order of Merit for National Foundation in 1968, becoming the first foreign national to receive the recognition for contributions to Korea’s independence movement.
 Dilkusha was designated a National Registered Cultural Heritage in 2017 and now operates as a branch of the Seoul Museum of History.
 By Park Jin-hai Published Nov 19, 2026 12:00 pm KST
 Japanese soldiers lure residents into a chapel before setting it on fire in a scene from the tvN drama "100 Days of Deception" reminiscent of the Jeam-ri Massacre of April 15, 1919. Courtesy of CJ ENM
 What makes tvN's hit series "100 Days of Deception" resonate so deeply with viewers is a dramatic narrative is firmly anchored in historical truths and real figures from the past. 
 Set in 1932 during the Japanese colonial period, the drama follows Lee Ga-kyung (Kim You-jung), a pickpocket who cares only about her own survival and escaping to America, who is blackmailed into working with anti-Japanese independence organization Gugukdan to infiltrate the Japanese Government-General of Korea for a 100-day mission. 
 Kim Hyun-joo draws a gun in a scene from tvN drama "100 Days of Deception." Courtesy of CJ ENM
 The drama truly begins when Ga-kyung is manipulated into joining Gugukdan. One of the group's core members is sniper Yoo So-ran (Kim Hyun-joo), who joined the independence movement after losing her daughter in the "Gyeam-ri Massacre" — a fictionalized depiction of a historical massacre that took place at Jeam-ri in 1919. 
 So-ran disguises herself as the wife of Korean American correspondent Philip Yoo (Lee Mu-saeng) to assassinate Sato Shinichi (Jin Seon-kyu), the man who orchestrated the massacre and rose to become the second-in-command of the Japanese government in Korea.
 In the drama, when Ga-kyung dismisses the anti-Japanese struggle as a "meaningless death," So-ran firmly retorts, "Even if one isn't Korean, no one considers dying while fighting for their country's independence a meaningless death." 
 The late Jeon Dong-rye, a survivor of the Jeam-ri Massacre, stands at the site of the Jeam Church in Gyeonggi Province. She was 21 years old at the time of the incident, which claimed her husband's life. She spent her post-liberation life testifying to the horrors of the Jeam-ri Massacre. Based on her detailed testimony in 1982, excavation and investigation work was carried out, leading to the recovery of the remains of 23 victims. Korea Times file 
 Jeam-ri Massacre 
 The Jeam-ri Massacre took place on April 15, 1919, in the village of Jeam-ri in what is now Hwaseong, Gyeonggi Province. Following the nationwide March 1 Independence Movement, resistance to Japanese rule was particularly fierce in the Suwon and Hwaseong areas.
 As a brutal act of retaliation, a detachment of the Imperial Japanese Army led by Lieutenant Arita Toshio deliberately targeted the village. Japanese soldiers gathered local Korean residents — predominantly Christians and Cheondoists, who were followers of a pantheistic religion — inside the Jeam-ri Village Church under false pretenses. They locked the doors, opened fire into the crowd and then set the church and neighboring homes on fire to destroy evidence and eliminate survivors. 
 According to historical records, 29 people were killed in total, including 23 at Jeam Church and six in the nearby village of Goju-ri.
 Lee Mu-saeng, left, plays western journalist Philip Yoo, a character inspired by Canadian missionary Frank W. Schofield. Courtesy of CJ ENM/ Ministry of Patriots & Veterans Affairs 
 Frank W. Schofield 
 The character of Philip Yoo draws clear inspiration from two real-life international journalists and activists who courageously exposed Japan's atrocities to the world: Frank W. Schofield, known in Korea as Seok Ho-pil, a Canadian missionary and veterinary pathologist who documented the aftermath of the Jeam-ri Massacre, and Albert Wilder Taylor, an AP temporary correspondent who reported on the March 1st Movement and the massacre before facing persecution and expulsion by Japanese authorities.
 Schofield visited the site shortly after the tragedy, documenting the destruction and photographing the victims. Schofield worked with foreign diplomats to publish detailed accounts overseas, bringing global attention to the harsh brutality of Japanese colonial rule in Korea. 
 Schofield's report, titled "The Massacre of Chai-Amm-Ni," was published in the May 27, 1919 edition of the Shanghai-based English-language newspaper The Shanghai Gazette, appearing as an article sent by an anonymous special correspondent in Seoul. Around the same time, his "Report of the Su-chon Atrocities" was secretly sent abroad and published in the July 26, 1919 edition of the American Presbyterian periodical, The Presbyterian Witness. 
 In 1968, he was awarded the Order of Merit for National Foundation by the Korean government, becoming the very first foreign national to receive this high-level recognition for contributions to Korea's independence movement. 
 The top photo shows the western-style mansion Huiwon (Garden of Joy) as seen in the tvN drama "100 Days of Deception," while the bottom photo shows Dilkusha, the restored home of Albert Taylor, the first U.S. journalist to report on the March 1, 1919, independence movement. Courtesy of CJ ENM, Yonhap
 Albert Taylor and Dilkusha 
 Albert Taylor/ Courtesy of Independence Hall of Korea
 The Western-style mansion Huiwon ("garden of joy"), which serves as the characters' clandestine base in the drama, is a direct homage to Dilkusha, the residence of Albert Taylor and his wife in Haengchon-dong, Jongno District, Seoul, whose Persian name translates to "heart's delight."
 Dilkusha's legacy is tied to Taylor's courageous journalism, which exposed Japanese colonial atrocities to the world. The AP correspondent played a pivotal role in smuggling the 1919 Declaration of Independence abroad after discovering it at Severance Hospital during his son's birth. He also took a huge risk by reporting on the brutal Jeam-ri Massacre.
 Taylor and his wife were expelled by the Japanese in 1942. Their home was designated a National Registered Cultural Heritage in 2017 and now operates as a branch of the Seoul Museum of History.
 By referencing the real history of the period, "100 Days of Deception" transforms historical pain into a powerful tribute to Korea's independence struggle.
